en: Theragāthā 16.2,
Vīsatinipāta, Paṭhamavagga (The First Chapter) [The verse would follow here]
The Verse of the Elder Pārāpariya:
“A thought arose in the recluse,
the bhikkhu Pārāpariya:”
For a man sitting alone,
secluded and meditating,
what is the successive sequence?
What vow, what conduct— acting according to one's own duty and not harming anyone?
The faculties of human beings lead to their welfare and their harm;
when unguarded, they lead to harm.
And for one's own welfare.
Guarding the very faculties, and protecting the faculties;
One who performs their own duty and does not harm anyone—
if such a person’s faculty of sight [is directed] toward forms, [it is well-restrained].
Not restraining one who is going away,
and failing to see the danger,
such a person is indeed not released from suffering.
If one does not restrain the ear-faculty from going toward sounds,
being one who fails to see the danger, [suffering will arise].
He is not released from suffering,
for he does not see the escape,
even if he indulges in fragrances.
One who is infatuated with fragrances is not released from suffering.
[Whether it be] sour or sweet-tasting—
Recalling bitter tastes,
one who is gripped by craving for flavors does not understand the heart.
Recalling pleasant tactile sensations that are not repulsive,
one who is impassioned, on account of that passion—
He experiences manifold suffering—
he who is unable to guard his mind against these mental states.
Then suffering follows it because of all these five [factors]:
filled with pus and blood,
Of many corpses, the lovely deed performed by Naravīra was like a decorated casket.
Bitter yet sweet in taste,
painful though bound by pleasure—
like a razor blade smeared with honey.
Scratching [the surface], one does not understand:
the female form, the female voice,
and even the touch of a woman.
One who is passionately attached to the scents of women experiences manifold suffering.
All the streams of women—
The five flow into the five;
only one who possesses energy is able to create an obstruction for them.
Thus he is one who possesses meaning, who stands in the Dhamma,
who is skillful, and who is discerning;
even while enjoying himself, he would act [righteously].
A duty that accords with the Dhamma and the goal is what should be done;
however, a duty connected with what is blameworthy is fruitless and leads to ruin.
Thinking, “This is not my task,” one who is discerning should remain heedful regarding that which is connected with one’s welfare.
And whatever delight is found in the Dhamma—
taking that up, you should practice it,
for that indeed is the supreme delight.
By various means, high and low, one seeks to overcome others; having struck them down,
slain them, or even caused them grief.
He who, out of recklessness, oppresses others—
just as a strong man, striking pin with pin, drives it home.
In the same way, the skillful one destroys [the unwholesome] by means of the faculties and non-faculties:
faith, energy, and concentration.
Cultivating mindfulness and wisdom,
having destroyed the five [hindrances] by means of the five [faculties],
the brahmin goes free from distress.
Thus he was one who spoke with purpose and stood firm in the Dhamma,
having followed the instruction of the Buddha's words in every single way.
“Such a person prospers in happiness.
… The Elder Pārāpariya…
